title: Adjectives or Adverbs as Modifiers
subtitle: Which form, and how to decide.
objectives: Choose between an adjective and an adverb
Modify an adjective with an adverb
Fix a sentence where the wrong form is used

cards.title: Adjective or adverb is decided by what it attaches to
cards.text: Not by how the word sounds. Find what is being described, and the form follows.

cards.title: What is it describing?
cards.text: A thing, or an action? That single question settles almost every case.
points: **Describing a noun** → adjective. *a quick lap*.
**Describing a verb** → adverb. *he drove quickly*.
**'He drove quick'** describes him, not the driving.
**Ask what the word points at.**

question.explain: It describes how he finished, which is the verb, so it takes the adverb.

cards.title: What is the word pointing at?
cards.text: Three decisions. Each wrong pick shows you what that sentence would mean.

cards.title: The pair that catches everyone
cards.text: Good is an adjective. Well is its adverb. And also an adjective meaning healthy.
points: **He is a good fighter.** Describes the fighter.
**He fights well.** Describes the fighting.
**'He fights good'** is the common error.
**'I am well'** means healthy, and is correct.

question.explain: 'Plays' is a verb, so it needs the adverb: she plays well.

cards.title: A review uses both, a line apart
cards.text: The thing and the doing get different words, and reviewers are careful about it.
points: **A smooth engine.** Adjective, describing the engine.
**It pulls smoothly.** Adverb, describing the pulling.
**Good brakes.** **Brakes well.**
**Swap them** and it reads as a mistake.

cards.title: An adverb can describe an adjective too
cards.text: This is where words like very, really and slightly live.
points: **A very fast lap.** 'Very' describes 'fast'.
**Slightly worn tyres.**
**Those adverbs modify the adjective**, not the verb.
**Three layers** are possible: *really quite quickly*.

cards.title: Describing a fault needs both forms
cards.text: What is wrong, and how it is behaving, take different words.
points: **A noisy bearing.** Adjective. The bearing is noisy.
**It runs noisily.** Adverb. The running is noisy.
**A slow blade** versus **it turns slowly.**
**Both sentences are true.** They describe different things.

question.explain: It describes how it runs, so an adverb.

cards.title: A fast car, driven fast
cards.alt: The same car parked and perfectly sharp beside the same car mid-corner with the background streaked into motion blur
cards.text: Left points at the car. Right points at the driving. Same word, two jobs.

cards.title: Literature Review: Don Quixote, Chapter 20: The Knight of the Mirrors
cards.text: A neighbour disguises himself as a rival knight, hoping to defeat Quixote and send him home.
points: **A brave knight.** Adjective.
**He fought bravely.** Adverb.
**The plan works badly**, which is the pattern of the book.
**Cervantes uses both** within single paragraphs.

terms.def: Describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb.
Any word adding detail to another.
A verb like 'is' or 'seems' that takes an adjective, not an adverb.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Describing a thing takes an adjective; describing an action takes an adverb.
Good is the adjective, well is the adverb.
Very and really describe adjectives, not verbs.
Ask what the word points at and the form follows.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 10 English, the last teaching week, and the one that makes weeks 7 to 9 usable. The whole lesson runs on one question (what is the word pointing at) because that single test resolves nearly every adjective-or-adverb decision without any further rules. Good and well get their own card since the error is common and socially noticeable. Adverbs modifying adjectives are included because 'very' and 'really' are used constantly and almost never understood as adverbs. The fault-description card pairs the two forms on the same object so the difference is visible rather than abstract.
discussion: What single question decides adjective or adverb?
What is 'very' doing in 'a very fast lap'?
extension: Describe a faulty object twice: once with an adjective, once with an adverb.
Find three uses of 'very' and say what each one modifies.
misconceptions: Using an adjective where an adverb is needed.
